prompt.context: You have 20 minutes to prepare a presentation to give to a CEO of a media company. The client has the No. 1 electronic components catalog, distributed at no cost to product designers. Revenues come from ads in the catalog. The CEO has noticed that revenues have declined 60% year over year. The CEO feels that because of the quality of the product, they are a content service provider. He is interested in converting the catalog into an online publication. He has come to you to determine if this business makes sense and how he should market it.
prompt.question: Does it make business sense to convert the electronic components catalog to an online publication, and how should the company market it?

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have editorial freedom?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they have editorial freedom and are not tied to the products they advertise.

clarifying_info.q: How is the content used by customers?
clarifying_info.a: The content is used by designers to determine specifications of components that may be used in product designs. The information is well-respected and typically seen as valuable to developers.

clarifying_info.q: How would ad revenue change online?
clarifying_info.a: The company would not get as much ad revenue from an online product, because advertisers would not pay as much for online ads.

clarifying_info.q: How would they monetize if they go online?
clarifying_info.a: They would have to change to a subscription or pay model, meaning developers would have to pay to access the information.

clarifying_info.q: Are there existing competitors in the online space?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, two competitors: Competitor A has been in business for 2 years with 75% market share — they are an electronics distributor whose reliability is questionable due to conflicts of interest. Competitor B has been in business for 1 year with 25% market share — they have the same data but at a higher price point and lack the functionality (search capabilities) of our client.
No, two competitors already exist online, but our client is first among truly independent content providers.

clarifying_info.q: What are the operational implications of going online?
clarifying_info.a: Because it is online, the information will have to be updated more frequently. The inventory needs of developers can be relayed to manufacturers, which may be valuable.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Operating Income Trend
exhibits.shows: A graph showing the company's revenue and operating income across three years (Y1, Y2, Y3)

framework: Market Entry Assessment: Who is already in the online space? What are competitors doing and how is our client differentiated?
Capabilities Assessment: Does the client have the staff, funding, sales force, and marketing capabilities to execute the transition?
Revenue Model: How does shifting from ad-based to subscription/pay model affect revenues and margins?
Financial Feasibility: Can the client recover upfront investment within the required time horizon?
Marketing Strategy: How should the online product be positioned and sold to developers?

questions.prompt: Assess the competitive landscape for the online electronic components catalog market.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: Competitor A (75% share, 2 years, electronics distributor with credibility/conflict-of-interest problem) and Competitor B (25% share, 1 year, same data but higher price and weaker search). Client differentiators: editorial independence, superior search functionality, lower price point than Competitor B, and trusted brand among designers.

questions.prompt: Based on the revenue trend shown in the exhibit, describe what is happening to the business.
questions.guidance: Revenues have been growing (120M → 160M → 240M) but operating income has been collapsing (110M → 80M → 40M). The gap shows costs growing much faster than revenue, or that the revenue growth is masking deep margin erosion. The 60% YoY revenue decline mentioned by the CEO suggests a more recent sharp drop not fully shown in the 3-year historical graph — likely the catalyst for the pivot.

math.setup: Operating margin trend: Y1 = 110/120 ≈ 92%, Y2 = 80/160 = 50%, Y3 = 40/240 ≈ 17%. Revenue declined 60% YoY in the most recent period.
steps: Margin compression of ~75 percentage points over 3 years signals structural cost or pricing problems
math.answer: Operating margins have collapsed from ~92% to ~17% over 3 years despite revenue growth, indicating severe structural deterioration.

questions.prompt: The consulting partner has made the recommendation to enter the online market. The company says they will move forward only if they can recover a $6M initial investment within 3 years. Estimate whether this is feasible.
questions.guidance: Use the provided market size proxy (total online market revenues), client's estimated 15% market share per year, and 10% operating margin to compute cumulative operating income over 3 years. Compare to $6M threshold.

math.setup: Total online market revenue is implied by the competitor revenues. Client estimated to capture 15% market share each year and operate at 10% margin. The case states the result was $18M, $24M, and $36M in years 1, 2, 3 respectively, with cumulative operating income of $7.8M over three years.
steps: Year 1 revenue: implied total market × 15% share = $18M
math.answer: Cumulative operating income of $7.8M over 3 years exceeds the $6M investment hurdle. The project is financially feasible.

brainstorming.prompt: What capabilities and considerations does the client need to address to successfully convert to an online subscription model?

categories.name: Technology & Product
ideas: Build or acquire robust online platform with advanced search
Ensure real-time or frequent data updates for component specifications
Develop API integrations to relay developer inventory needs to manufacturers
Mobile and cross-platform accessibility

categories.name: Monetization & Pricing
ideas: Design subscription tiers (individual, team, enterprise)
Freemium model to ease developer adoption
Per-query or per-download pay-per-use pricing
Bundle with manufacturer data feeds as premium offering

categories.name: Sales & Marketing
ideas: Leverage existing No. 1 brand reputation among designers
Target engineering teams at OEM companies directly
Partner with component manufacturers for co-marketing
Content marketing through technical whitepapers and webinars

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Hire editorial and data team to increase update frequency
Establish data quality and accuracy processes to differentiate from Competitor A
Customer support for subscription users
Build feedback loop from developers to improve content

categories.name: Risks & Mitigation
ideas: Developer resistance to paying for previously free content
Competitor A response (price cuts, data deals)
Reliability of subscription revenue vs. ad revenue
Data privacy and IP protection online

recommendation: The client should proceed with converting to an online subscription model. Their core competency — providing high-quality, independent electronic component specifications — is directly transferable online and is not being violated by the model change.

They are sufficiently differentiated from existing competitors: Competitor A has credibility issues due to conflicts of interest, and Competitor B charges more and has inferior search functionality. The client can compete on trust, price, and product quality.
The financial case is positive: estimated cumulative operating income of $7.8M over 3 years exceeds the $6M investment threshold.
risks: Developers may resist paying for information that was previously free
Online ad revenues will be lower, making the subscription model critical to success
Competitors may respond aggressively (price cuts, partnerships) once client enters
next_steps: Finalize subscription pricing model and tier structure
Build or license the online platform with advanced search capabilities
Develop a go-to-market plan targeting existing catalog users with introductory pricing
Establish data update frequency and editorial processes for online publication
